sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**

None. All eight lines are yes.

One finding has no checklist line. It comes from the copy rules for deadlines in `agents/critic.md` ("The words are part of the design"), so the director can decide whether to use it:

1. **A deadline line can be read two ways.** This is the second paragraph, about y 310–420: "all tickets must be **collected by four** or the prizes go back in the box."
   - **Reading 1:** winners must claim their prizes with their tickets by four.
   - **Reading 2:** the organisers must collect the ticket stubs by four.
   - **What goes wrong:** a winner who takes the second reading turns up after four and loses their prize. That is exactly the kind of thing people hold the organisers to afterwards.
   - **Same problem in paragraph one:** "by the time the gates open" (y 178) is a deadline with no time. "The trestle by the door" doesn't say which door.
   - **Fix:** say who does what by when, for example "Winners: claim your prize with your ticket by 4 pm, or it goes back in the box." Give the gate-opening time.
   - Defect (common sense, no catalog entry). Weight: minor to major. The layout is fine, but this notice exists to carry these rules, so a misread rule is a real failure of its job.

**What's working.**
- **The headline names the whole job.** "Notes for the summer fete" (180–760, y 85–130) tells a stranger at once what this is and that it is practical. Nothing else competes with it.
- **Nothing extra.** There are no rules, boxes, icons or decoration, just a heading and two short paragraphs. That suits a quick notice, and every mark on the page carries information.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** None.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

Note for the director: key facts are emphasised two ways. "three o'clock sharp" is italic (517–712, y 324), but "collected by four" is bold (180–378, y 365), even though both are times. I checked the consistency line's entry ("Repeated elements follow one program"). It covers repeated components like cards, buttons and headings, not emphasis inside a paragraph, so I filed the line as yes. The mixed emphasis belongs to the Text section critic.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Separate from the checklist, one thing for the director. The body uses two kinds of emphasis that don't match how important each item is. The two times are set differently: "arrive before ten" (about x 258–430, y 178) and "three o'clock sharp" (about x 517–715, y 324) are italic, which hardly shows when you scan. "collected by four", "labelled with their ingredients" and "on the field only" are bold, which stands out. Someone scanning only the bold gets the ticket deadline and the parking rule, and can miss the arrival time and the draw time. Five phrases are emphasised in six lines of body text, so the emphasis also loses force. The fix is to give every time or deadline the same treatment, use bold only for what a reader must act on, and drop the italic stress. This is taste, minor, and probably belongs under `text` (emphasis). No hierarchy line fails on it, because the title is still clearly where the eye starts.

**What's working.**
- The title "Notes for the summer fete" (x 180–760, y 85–130) is bold and about twice the body size, with clear space under it. The eye starts there without any doubt.
- There are only two levels, title and body, with a big step between them. Nothing sits in between to blur them, which is the right amount of structure for a short note.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** It isn't. The same problem also fails **Do the main divisions of the frame follow one proportion…?**
   - **Where:** The text column runs from x≈180 to about x≈980–1000 on a 1280 px frame. That leaves roughly 180 px on the left and about 280–300 px on the right.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The column is too close to the middle to read as a choice to sit left, and too far off to be centered. It looks like a centered container that slipped about 50–60 px left, so the page looks a little unfinished. The three splits (left margin, column, right margin) follow no proportion you could name.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, chapter "Balance": a placement that is neither clearly here nor clearly there makes the eye waver. Proportional division is a soft guide (Tschichold, *The Form of the Book*), so that part is taste.
   - **Fix:** Pick one. Either center the column on the frame, or move it clearly to one side and size the margins by a simple ratio, such as a left margin equal to the line spacing times a whole number, or a 1:2 split of the two margins.
   - **Type:** Convention (near-miss alignment) and taste (proportion). **Weight: minor.** The notice still reads fine.
2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** It doesn't.
   - **Where:** All the ink sits in the upper left quadrant, in rows ~85–420 and columns ~180–980. Rows ~420–800, almost half the frame, are empty, and nothing on the right or at the bottom balances the dark headline.
   - **What the viewer sees:** In this still the page looks top-heavy and pushed toward the upper left. That is normal for a web page that scrolls, but on a printed or pinned notice it would look like content is missing.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, chapter "Balance": a heavy side needs a counterweight.
   - **Fix:** If this is a web page, leave the top anchor alone. Fixing finding 1 removes most of the lopsided look. If it will be printed or shown as a single screen, move the block down so it sits a little above center, or give the lower area a deliberate role, such as a contact or date line.
   - **Type:** Taste, depending on the medium. **Weight: minor.**

**What's working.**
- **Spacing shows the grouping.** Lines are about 41 px apart and paragraphs about 65 px apart, and the headline sits closer to its body text than to the top edge. The two rule groups (setup and cakes, then raffle and parking) read as separate units at a glance, with no rules or boxes needed.
- **One left edge.** The headline and both paragraphs hang from the same x≈180 line, so the eye path runs straight down with no detours.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether this is a scrolling web page or a fixed print or screen size. That decides whether the empty lower half is the normal end of a page or a balance problem. I also couldn't see how the column behaves at other widths.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (exact alignment or a clear break; visual weight balances; one proportion for the main divisions)

I've finished checking the Text section. Here is the report.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Are quotation marks curly, and are dashes and ellipses the true characters?** No. The apostrophe in "o'clock" (second paragraph, about x 590–600, y 315–330) is a straight typewriter mark, not a curly apostrophe. At this size most readers won't notice it. It is still the only typographic detail on the page that looks unfinished next to an otherwise careful serif setting. My reference doesn't settle straight versus curly quotes from a checked source (Bringhurst covers dashes and spacing, not this), so treat this as common sense rather than a rule. Fix: use a true apostrophe (’) here, and turn on smart quotes wherever this copy comes from. **Convention / taste. Minor.**

**Outside the checklist (for the director).** Italic and bold do the same job here. "*arrive before ten*" and "*three o'clock sharp*" are italic, but "**collected by four**" is bold, and all three are times or deadlines. "**labelled with their ingredients**" and "**on the field only**" are bold rules. That makes five emphasised phrases in five lines of text. A reader can't tell what the difference between italic and bold means, and so much bold flattens what's important, so the actual deadlines don't stand out. Direction: choose one signal for the things people must act on (times and rules), and use less of it. **Taste. Minor to major depending on how much the hierarchy critic weighs it.** Copy: "fete" is missing the circumflex (fête). That's acceptable in British usage and only worth checking against house style.

**What's working.**
- **Clean, well-spaced body text.** It's a single readable serif at a comfortable size with generous leading (about 41 px per line). It's set flush left with an even rag, and the space between paragraphs stays clearly larger than the space between lines. The short notice reads in one easy pass.
- **Heading and body from one family.** The heading is a heavy weight of the same family, set tight on one line, so the page reads as one plan with a clear step from title to text.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Lines run at about 75–76 characters, the top of Bringhurst's 45–75 range, at this window width. Check that the column has a maximum width so the lines don't get longer in a wider window.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (quotation marks and apostrophes curly)

Walk (working notes). First read: the eye lands on the heading, then jumps to the bold phrases. It's a short notice for volunteers at a village fete. Colour: near-black text on white, with no hue anywhere.

- Small palette: yes
- Saturated colour kept to a small share: yes (there is none)
- Clear range of light and dark: yes (dark text on white, so the structure survives in grayscale)
- Warm forward, cool back: yes (no hue is used)
- Matching colours look the same: yes
- No edges that seem to vibrate: yes
- Status colours keep their usual meaning: yes (there are none)
- Colour never the only signal: yes (emphasis comes from bold and italic, not colour)
- Dark theme not pure black: yes (this is a light page, so the line doesn't apply)

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece is only neutral colours, near-black text on a white page.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Contrast.** All the text, from the heading at about y 85–130 to the body at y 165–420, is one near-black (it looks like a very dark gray, not pure #000) on white. The contrast is clearly well above 4.5:1, and the page reads the same in grayscale. That suits a practical notice people have to act on.
- **Emphasis without colour.** The key instructions ("labelled with their ingredients", "collected by four", "on the field only") and the times ("arrive before ten", "three o'clock sharp") stand out through bold and italic, not colour. The emphasis survives colour-vision deficiency, grayscale printing and photocopying, which is likely for a fete notice. Whether bold and italic are the right way to split the emphasis belongs to the text and hierarchy critics, not here.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
